title: LIMIT, OFFSET, and Keyset Pagination
description: Compare classic LIMIT/OFFSET with SQL-standard FETCH FIRST and implement high-performance keyset pagination.

data.text: Limiting result set size is essential for API pagination and user interfaces. PostgreSQL supports both the traditional `LIMIT / OFFSET` syntax and the SQL:2008 standard `FETCH FIRST ... ROWS ONLY` syntax.
Syntax Comparison: LIMIT vs FETCH FIRST

data.title: PostgreSQL LIMIT vs SQL Standard FETCH
data.content: Both produce identical execution plans in PostgreSQL.
data.code:
-- PostgreSQL native syntax
SELECT id, title FROM articles
ORDER BY published_at DESC
LIMIT 10 OFFSET 20;

-- SQL:2008 Standard syntax
SELECT id, title FROM articles
ORDER BY published_at DESC
OFFSET 20 ROWS
FETCH NEXT 10 ROWS ONLY;

data.text: The High Cost of Deep Offsets & The Keyset Solution

When executing `OFFSET 500000 LIMIT 10`, PostgreSQL must physically scan 500,000 rows through an index or table before returning the 10 target rows. Keyset pagination (cursor-based pagination) eliminates this by seeking directly to the next row via an index seek predicate.

data.title: Keyset (Cursor-Based) Pagination Query
data.content: Runs in constant O(1) time regardless of whether you are on page 1 or page 50,000.
data.code:
-- Page 1: Initial query
SELECT id, title, created_at FROM articles
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 10;

-- Page 2: Fetch rows using cursor (last_created_at, last_id)
SELECT id, title, created_at FROM articles
WHERE (created_at, id) < ('2024-01-01 10:00:00'::timestamptz, 'art-123')
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 10;

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: `LIMIT` and `FETCH FIRST` restrict the number of rows returned.
`OFFSET` skips rows but suffers severe performance degradation on large tables.
Use keyset pagination (`WHERE (col, id) < (cursor_col, cursor_id)`) for scalable feeds.
